analysis.one_liner: Hands nearly all federal Bureau of Land Management land over to the states.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Natural Resources subcommittee from April 1994 until the Congress ended, backed by 26 House Republicans and no Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Interior Department to offer every piece of land managed by the Bureau of Land Management — roughly 270 million acres, mostly in Western states — to the state it sits in, with the transfer taking effect in 1998. A state would have to take all the land or none of it. States would have to honor every existing grazing permit, lease, and mining claim. Land not under a lease or permit could only be used for public purposes and would return to the federal government if misused. Wilderness areas, wilderness study areas, and certain environmentally sensitive or contaminated lands were exempted. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main winners would be extractive industries operating on BLM land — hardrock mining claim holders, ranchers with federal grazing permits, and oil and gas lessees — because state governments historically manage land to produce revenue, with lower grazing fees, lighter environmental review, and faster permitting than the federal government. State governments would also gain title to the land itself, including subsurface estates and water rights. Some Western-state officials who resent federal ownership would gain local control. Ordinary people who hunt, hike, camp, or graze on these lands would face a patchwork: access and environmental protection would depend entirely on each state's priorities, and the bill guaranteed favorable terms to existing mining and grazing interests before any state even decided.

how_it_helps.text: Mining claim holders would keep their claims, now enforced by the state, under management historically more favorable to mining than federal oversight.
Ranchers holding federal grazing permits would deal with state land offices, which typically charge lower grazing fees than the federal government.
Oil, gas, and other lessees would have their federal leases and permits honored by the states for the full term.
States taking the lands would gain title to surface, subsurface, and water rights — an asset base they could manage for revenue.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on ordinary Americans: 270 million acres of land owned by everyone would be managed under 50 different state priorities, with guaranteed rights for mining claims and grazing permits baked in from day one. Taxpayers nationwide would lose the federal stewardship rules that govern the land today, and states free to maximize revenue could graze, mine, or develop acreage the public currently uses for recreation and habitat. The public-purpose covenant offered only a partial backstop, and enforcing it through reversion would take years.

drawbacks.text: Western states genuinely bear costs from federal land ownership: no property tax on those acres, plus management burdens and payment-in-lieu-of-taxes dependence, and state and local officials argue they can manage nearby land more responsively than a distant federal agency.

The bill included safeguards — wilderness, wilderness study areas, and areas of critical environmental concern were exempt, and unleased land would revert to the United States if not used for public purposes — but the reversion clause is a weak check: it only triggers after a state has already misused the land.

The all-or-nothing structure means a state could not pick and choose; a state that wanted the land would also absorb management and fire costs on hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of acreage it might not be equipped to steward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill was real: Western states carry costs of managing around federal land without a property-tax base, and local voices have little say in how neighboring BLM acreage is used. But the bill's own design shows its tilt — states would have had to honor every existing mining claim and lease, while the only conservation shield was a "public purpose" covenant enforceable mainly through reversion years after a state made its choices. Given how states historically manage their own trust lands — for revenue, through grazing, mining, and development — the likely result was weaker environmental standards and cheaper extraction on land that belongs to all Americans, with wilderness and study-area exemptions the strongest safeguard in the bill. The costs to the public outweighed the local-control gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to a subcommittee, and the Interior Department was asked for its views, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Craig Thomas introduced H.R. 4157 on March 24, 1994 with 25 Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on March 24, 1994, and on April 27, 1994 was referred further to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands.
On May 25, 1994 the committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department, but the bill never advanced to a markup or a vote.
The 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 with the bill still stuck in subcommittee, so it died without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary Americans who use and value the public lands are better off, because the roughly 270 million acres of BLM land stayed under national management with uniform environmental and access rules. The extractive industries that would have gained from state control got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Craig Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 24, 1994 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 25 of 176 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 25 were Republicans, mostly from Western and mountain states.

against.name: National conservation groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed wholesale disposal of federal public land to the states, arguing state control would open it to mining, drilling, grazing, and sale.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Majority control of the committee of jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: The Democratic-led committee of jurisdiction never reported the bill or scheduled a markup; it was referred to subcommittee and stayed there.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans in a House controlled by Democrats, who chaired the Natural Resources Committee the bill was sent to; the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Their existing mining claims would be honored by state governments, and states generally manage land to maximize revenue with lighter environmental review than the BLM. Mining on public land already returns little to the Treasury; state control would tend to deepen that deal.

State land offices historically charge far lower grazing fees than the federal government, so a transfer would effectively subsidize ranching on land the public owns, at taxpayer and land-health expense.

Existing federal leases and permits would carry over to state administration, where permitting tends to be faster and environmental conditions lighter. Drilling and extraction decisions would move out of national oversight.

Roughly 270 million acres of BLM land support hunting, fishing, camping, and off-road recreation that anchors Western economies. State management could loosen or tighten access depending on the state, but the loss of a uniform national guarantee of public access was the real risk.
